claim: Voltage-gated ion channels play a fundamental role in the generation and propagation of electrical signals in excitable cells and muscle tissues.
source: Voltage-gated ion channels play a fundamental role in a wide range of physiological processes, including the generation and propagation of electrical signals in excitable cells and muscle tissues, neurotransmitter release in pre-synaptic nerve endings, and maintaining cell homeostasis (Hille, 1978).

claim: Voltage-gated ion channels play a fundamental role in neurotransmitter release in pre-synaptic nerve endings.
source: Voltage-gated ion channels play a fundamental role in a wide range of physiological processes, including the generation and propagation of electrical signals in excitable cells and muscle tissues, neurotransmitter release in pre-synaptic nerve endings, and maintaining cell homeostasis (Hille, 1978).

claim: Voltage-gated ion channels play a fundamental role in maintaining cell homeostasis.
source: Voltage-gated ion channels play a fundamental role in a wide range of physiological processes, including the generation and propagation of electrical signals in excitable cells and muscle tissues, neurotransmitter release in pre-synaptic nerve endings, and maintaining cell homeostasis (Hille, 1978).

claim: Voltage-gated ion channels comprise four subunits of each six transmembrane segments (S1–S6).
source: They comprise four subunits of each six transmembrane segments (S1–S6), which are assembled into two functionally distinct parts: a central ion-selective pore formed by the combined S5 and S6 segments of four domains, surrounded by four voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) formed by the four helices S1–S4.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about voltage-gated ion channels

claim: The central ion-selective pore is formed by the combined S5 and S6 segments of four domains.
source: They comprise four subunits of each six transmembrane segments (S1–S6), which are assembled into two functionally distinct parts: a central ion-selective pore formed by the combined S5 and S6 segments of four domains, surrounded by four voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) formed by the four helices S1–S4.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about voltage-gated ion channels

claim: Four voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) are formed by the four helices S1–S4.
source: They comprise four subunits of each six transmembrane segments (S1–S6), which are assembled into two functionally distinct parts: a central ion-selective pore formed by the combined S5 and S6 segments of four domains, surrounded by four voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) formed by the four helices S1–S4.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about voltage-gated ion channels

claim: S4 is considered the principal component of voltage sensing because it contains positively charged residues that are periodically aligned at every third position.
source: S4 is considered the principal component of voltage sensing because it contains positively charged residues that are periodically aligned at every third position.
evidence: Established knowledge about voltage sensing in ion channels

claim: The first four arginines (R1-R4) of S4 sense and interact with the surrounding electric field.
source: The first four arginines (R1-R4) of S4 sense and interact with the surrounding electric field, and move the S4 outward during depolarization and inward during hyperpolarization in a combination of translation, rotation and tilt (Faure et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014a, 2014b; Vargas et al., 2012; Yarov-Yarovoy et al., 2012).

claim: S4 moves outward during depolarization and inward during hyperpolarization in a combination of translation, rotation and tilt.
source: The first four arginines (R1-R4) of S4 sense and interact with the surrounding electric field, and move the S4 outward during depolarization and inward during hyperpolarization in a combination of translation, rotation and tilt (Faure et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014a, 2014b; Vargas et al., 2012; Yarov-Yarovoy et al., 2012).

claim: S4 changes are mechanically transmitted to the pore domain via the S4–S5 linker and the C-terminal S6 of the same and neighboring subunit.
source: These changes are mechanically transmitted to the pore domain via the S4–S5 linker and the C-terminal S6 of the same and neighboring subunit, leading to gating of the central pore (Batulan et al., 2010; Wall-Lacelle et al., 2011; Haddad and Blunck, 2011; Muroi et al., 2010; Long et al., 2005b; Catterall, 2010; Bezanilla, 2005; Lu et al., 2001, 2002; Labro et al., 2008).

claim: Opening of the pore occurs in at least two steps.
source: Opening of the pore has been shown to occur in at least two steps (Del Camino et al., 2005; Kalstrup and Blunck, 2013).

claim: A direct structural and functional interaction between the VSD and pore has been demonstrated.
source: In addition to the coupling in this region, a direct structural and functional interaction between the VSD and pore has been demonstrated (Lee et al., 2009a; Li-Smerin et al., 2000; Petitjean et al., 2015).

claim: The VSD and pore domain make up modules that can be adapted to different scenarios.
source: The topology and structure of the Kv channels suggest that the VSD and pore domain make up modules that can be adapted to different scenarios (Blunck and Batulan, 2012; Kim et al., 2014).

claim: Chimeras of VSD of one and pore domain of another protein were able to gate in a voltage-dependent fashion.
source: Chimeras of VSD of one and pore domain of another protein were able to gate in a voltage-dependent fashion (Lu et al., 2001; Arrigoni et al., 2013).

claim: The VSD of Ci-VSP has been shown to function in the absence of the phosphatase.
source: It was possible to carry out structural studies on isolated voltage sensor domains (Li et al., 2014a; Chakrapani et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2003), and the VSD of Ci-VSP has been shown to function in the absence of the phosphatase (Labro et al., 2012; Murata et al., 2005).

claim: Voltage-gated proton channels (Hv) lack a separate pore domain altogether such that its VSD is directly responsible for proton permeation.
source: Finally, the voltage-gated proton channels (Hv) lack a separate pore domain altogether such that its VSD is directly responsible for proton permeation (Lee et al., 2009b; Li et al., 2015; Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006).

claim: Prolonged depolarization reconfigures VSDs of numerous voltage-gated proteins into a stable 'relaxed' state.
source: Prolonged depolarization has been shown to reconfigure VSDs of numerous voltage-gated proteins into a stable 'relaxed' state, resulting in a hyperpolarizing shift of the voltage dependence of both pore closure and return of the VSD to its resting position (Haddad and Blunck, 2011; Piper et al., 2003; Tan et al., 2012; Olcese et al., 1997; Kuzmenkin et al., 2004; Bruening-Wright and Larsson, 2007; Villalba-Galea et al., 2008).

claim: Relaxation results in a hyperpolarizing shift of the voltage dependence of both pore closure and return of the VSD to its resting position.
source: Prolonged depolarization has been shown to reconfigure VSDs of numerous voltage-gated proteins into a stable 'relaxed' state, resulting in a hyperpolarizing shift of the voltage dependence of both pore closure and return of the VSD to its resting position (Haddad and Blunck, 2011; Piper et al., 2003; Tan et al., 2012; Olcese et al., 1997; Kuzmenkin et al., 2004; Bruening-Wright and Larsson, 2007; Villalba-Galea et al., 2008).

claim: Relaxation or mode shift has been shown to be correlated with slow C-type inactivation.
source: Relaxation or mode shift has been shown to be influenced by the state of the pore domain; it was observed to be correlated with slow C-type inactivation (Olcese et al., 1997; Cuello et al., 2010; Männikkö et al., 2005) and pore stabilization in the open state (Haddad and Blunck, 2011).

claim: Relaxation or mode shift has been shown to be correlated with pore stabilization in the open state.
source: Relaxation or mode shift has been shown to be influenced by the state of the pore domain; it was observed to be correlated with slow C-type inactivation (Olcese et al., 1997; Cuello et al., 2010; Männikkö et al., 2005) and pore stabilization in the open state (Haddad and Blunck, 2011).

claim: Mode shift developed in Ci-VSP, which does not possess any pore domain, suggesting relaxation to be an intrinsic property of the VSD.
source: On the other hand, mode shift also developed in Ci-VSP, which does not possess any pore domain, suggesting relaxation to be an intrinsic property of the VSD (Labro et al., 2012; Villalba-Galea et al., 2008).

claim: The N-terminal tail may affect VSD relaxation in hERG channels.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the N-terminal tail (Tan et al., 2012) and S3-S4 linker length (Priest et al., 2013) may affect the VSD relaxation in hERG and Shaker channels, respectively.

claim: S3-S4 linker length may affect VSD relaxation in Shaker channels.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the N-terminal tail (Tan et al., 2012) and S3-S4 linker length (Priest et al., 2013) may affect the VSD relaxation in hERG and Shaker channels, respectively.

claim: Shaker-iVSD showed significantly altered gating kinetics compared to full-length Shaker channels.
source: Shaker-iVSD showed significantly altered gating kinetics and formed a cation-selective ion channel with a strong preference for protons.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the abstract

claim: Shaker-iVSD formed a cation-selective ion channel with a strong preference for protons.
source: Shaker-iVSD showed significantly altered gating kinetics and formed a cation-selective ion channel with a strong preference for protons.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the abstract

claim: Ion conduction in Shaker-iVSD developed despite identical primary sequence, indicating an allosteric influence of the pore domain.
source: Ion conduction in Shaker-iVSD developed despite identical primary sequence, indicating an allosteric influence of the pore domain.

claim: Shaker-iVSD displays pronounced 'relaxation'.
source: Shaker-iVSD also displays pronounced 'relaxation'.
evidence: Experimental observation reported in the abstract

claim: Closing of the pore correlates with entry into relaxation suggesting that the two processes are energetically related.
source: Closing of the pore correlates with entry into relaxation suggesting that the two processes are energetically related.

claim: Shaker-iVSD mutants were transiently expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes.
source: Shaker-iVSD mutants were transiently expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes, and their electrophysiological properties examined using the cut-open oocyte voltage-clamp technique (Batulan et al., 2010; Taglialatela et al., 1992).

claim: Gating currents arising from Shaker-iVSD were detected 4–5 days after cRNA injection using the cut-open oocyte technique.
source: Gating currents arising from Shaker-iVSD were detected 4–5 days after cRNA injection using the cut-open oocyte technique (Figure 1b, top).

claim: The gating currents of Shaker-iVSD could not be estimated reliably because of substantial ionic currents in particular when holding the potential at −90 mV.
source: However, unlike those observed in Shaker-W434F (Figure 1b bottom), the gating currents of Shaker-iVSD could not be estimated reliably because of substantial ionic currents in particular when holding the potential at −90 mV.

claim: The observed ionic currents in response to a series of 250 ms test pulses applied in 10 mV steps exhibited a weak voltage dependence.
source: The observed ionic currents in response to a series of 250 ms test pulses applied in 10 mV steps exhibited a weak voltage dependence (Figure 1c).

claim: At the depolarized holding potential of 0 mV, the currents exhibited strong rectification with inward currents at hyperpolarized potentials.
source: In contrast, at the depolarized holding potential of 0 mV, the currents exhibited strong rectification with inward currents at hyperpolarized potentials.

claim: The phenotype was consistent with an ion channel, conducting at negative membrane potentials and very slow activation and deactivation kinetics.
source: The phenotype was consistent with an ion channel, conducting at negative membrane potentials and very slow activation and deactivation kinetics (Figure 1c and f).

claim: No similar currents developed for Shaker-W434F at similar expression level.
source: We confirmed that no similar currents developed for Shaker-W434F at similar expression level (Figure 1d) and that endogenous currents were negligible in H2O-injected oocytes (Figure 1f).

claim: Endogenous currents were negligible in H2O-injected oocytes.
source: We confirmed that no similar currents developed for Shaker-W434F at similar expression level (Figure 1d) and that endogenous currents were negligible in H2O-injected oocytes (Figure 1f).

claim: Shaker-iVSD expressed in HEK293 cells shows the same ionic currents and voltage dependence as observed in Xenopus oocytes.
source: The resulting currents in whole-cell patch-clamp recordings show the same ionic currents and voltage dependence as observed in Xenopus oocytes (Figure 1e).

claim: Holding the membrane potential polarized (−90 mV) led to constitutively open channels in Shaker-iVSD.
source: Holding the membrane potential polarized (−90 mV) led, as in Xenopus oocytes, to constitutively open channels, whereas holding at 0 mV led to hyperpolarization-activated ionic currents with slightly less rectification than in Xenopus oocytes (Figure 1g).

claim: Holding at 0 mV led to hyperpolarization-activated ionic currents with slightly less rectification than in Xenopus oocytes.
source: Holding the membrane potential polarized (−90 mV) led, as in Xenopus oocytes, to constitutively open channels, whereas holding at 0 mV led to hyperpolarization-activated ionic currents with slightly less rectification than in Xenopus oocytes (Figure 1g).

claim: The inward currents increased and E(H+) shifted to more positive potentials when decreasing external pH, consistent with a proton selective pore.
source: Consistent with a proton selective pore, the inward currents increased and E(H+) shifted to more positive potentials when decreasing external pH, although the reversal potential did not reach E(H+) completely (12.5 ± 1.6 mV for pH 4.5 and −5.4 ± 1.8 mV for pH 9.5; Figure 2a).

claim: The reversal potential did not reach E(H+) completely (12.5 ± 1.6 mV for pH 4.5 and −5.4 ± 1.8 mV for pH 9.5).
source: Consistent with a proton selective pore, the inward currents increased and E(H+) shifted to more positive potentials when decreasing external pH, although the reversal potential did not reach E(H+) completely (12.5 ± 1.6 mV for pH 4.5 and −5.4 ± 1.8 mV for pH 9.5; Figure 2a).

claim: Substitution of NMDG+ with D-sorbitol in the external solution to a final concentration of 10 mM substantially decreased the normalized inward current and shifted the Vrev from −1 ± 1 mV to −62.5 ± 2.5 mV at symmetric pH = 7.35.
source: Substitution of NMDG+ with D-sorbitol in the external solution to a final concentration of 10 mM (versus 115 mM cytosolic) substantially decreased the normalized inward current and shifted the Vrev from −1 ± 1 mV to −62.5 ± 2.5 mV at symmetric pH = 7.35, suggesting that even NMDG+ ions are to a certain extent permeant charge carriers of Shaker-iVSD-induced currents (Figure 2b).

claim: NMDG+ ions are to a certain extent permeant charge carriers of Shaker-iVSD-induced currents.
source: Substitution of NMDG+ with D-sorbitol in the external solution to a final concentration of 10 mM (versus 115 mM cytosolic) substantially decreased the normalized inward current and shifted the Vrev from −1 ± 1 mV to −62.5 ± 2.5 mV at symmetric pH = 7.35, suggesting that even NMDG+ ions are to a certain extent permeant charge carriers of Shaker-iVSD-induced currents (Figure 2b).

claim: A proton gradient of pHin/pHout5.5/7.5 resulted in a Vrev −7.0 ± 1.1 mV.
source: A proton gradient of pHin/pHout5.5/7.5 and 4.5/7.5 at a low NMDG+ concentration (10 mM) and high buffer concentrations in both external and internal solutions resulted in a Vrev −7.0 ± 1.1 mV and −34.9 ± 1.8 mV, respectively (Figure 2c).

claim: A proton gradient of pHin/pHout4.5/7.5 resulted in a Vrev −34.9 ± 1.8 mV.
source: A proton gradient of pHin/pHout5.5/7.5 and 4.5/7.5 at a low NMDG+ concentration (10 mM) and high buffer concentrations in both external and internal solutions resulted in a Vrev −7.0 ± 1.1 mV and −34.9 ± 1.8 mV, respectively (Figure 2c).

claim: The relative permeability for protons over NMDG+ was PH/PNMDG ~ 1400 according to the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation.
source: The relative permeability for protons over NMDG+ was PH/PNMDG ~ 1400 according to the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data using established equation

claim: The experiments excluded any significant permeability for anions.
source: The experiments also excluded any significant permeability for anions (symmetric 10 mM).

claim: Normalized current amplitudes of Shaker-iVSD recorded in external solutions containing either Na+ or K+ as the predominant extracellular cation were 1.35 and 1.54 times higher than in NMDG+ containing external solution.
source: Normalized current amplitudes of Shaker-iVSD recorded in external solutions containing either Na+ or K+ as the predominant extracellular cation were 1.35 and 1.54 times higher than in NMDG+ containing external solution (Figure 2d–e).

claim: The order of permeation efficiency was P(H+) >> P(K+) ≈ P(Na+) > P(NMDG+).
source: The order of permeation efficiency was P(H+) >> P(K+) ≈ P(Na+) > P(NMDG+).

claim: Replacement of the anion mesylate (MeSO3−) with chloride in the external solution did not alter the Shaker-iVSD-induced current, confirming that the current is not carried by anions.
source: Replacement of the anion mesylate (MeSO3−) with chloride in the external solution (NMDG-MeSO3 vs NMDG-Cl) did not alter the Shaker-iVSD-induced current, confirming that the current is not carried by anions (Figure 2f).

claim: Ionic currents through the VSD of the Shaker channel have been described for protons and other cations upon mutations along the S4.
source: Ionic currents through the VSD of the Shaker channel have been described for protons and other cations upon mutations along the S4 (Starace and Bezanilla, 2004; Moreau et al., 2015; Tombola et al., 2005), and the transmembrane domain of Hv1 proton channels consist of only S1-S4 (Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006; Takeshita et al., 2014).

claim: The transmembrane domain of Hv1 proton channels consist of only S1-S4.
source: Ionic currents through the VSD of the Shaker channel have been described for protons and other cations upon mutations along the S4 (Starace and Bezanilla, 2004; Moreau et al., 2015; Tombola et al., 2005), and the transmembrane domain of Hv1 proton channels consist of only S1-S4 (Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006; Takeshita et al., 2014).

claim: Hv channels are blocked by Zn2+ in the micromolar range.
source: Since Hv channels are blocked by Zn2+ in the micromolar range (Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006), we tested Shaker-iVSD's sensitivity to the application of external Zn2+.

claim: With increasing concentrations of Zn2+ (0–20 µM), the ionic current of Shaker-iVSD continuously reduced.
source: We found that with increasing concentrations of Zn2+ (0–20 µM), the ionic current of Shaker-iVSD continuously reduced (Figure 3a and c).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3a and c

claim: The time course of the normalized fluorescence change did not alter during activation in the presence of Zn2+ but deactivation was slowed.
source: The time course of the normalized fluorescence change did not alter during activation in the presence of Zn2+ but deactivation was slowed (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3b and d

claim: The fluorescence voltage (FV) relation remained unaltered in the presence of Zn2+.
source: Accordingly, also the fluorescence voltage (FV) relation remained unaltered.

claim: The relative fluorescence change was diminished with increasing Zn2+-concentration similar to the decrease in current amplitude.
source: While the activation kinetics and FV remained unaltered, the relative fluorescence change was diminished with increasing Zn2+-concentration similar to the decrease in current amplitude (Figure 3b and e).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3b and e

claim: A reduced relative fluorescence change indicates that immobilization of the voltage sensor by Zn2+ caused the current decrease.
source: A reduced relative fluorescence change indicates that immobilization of the voltage sensor by Zn2+ caused the current decrease.

claim: In Hv1 channels, histidines at position H140 and H193 have been shown to be responsible for the Zn2+ sensitivity.
source: In Hv1 channels, histidines at position H140 and H193 have been shown to be responsible for the Zn2+ sensitivity (Ramsey et al., 2006; Takeshita et al., 2014).

claim: H140 and H193 in Hv1 align with F280 and E335 in Shaker-iVSD, respectively.
source: While the histidines are not conserved in Shaker-iVSD, H140 and H193 align with F280 and E335, respectively.

claim: The lower affinity of glutamate and aspartate might be responsible for the lower sensitivity of Shaker-iVSD to Zn2+.
source: The lower affinity of glutamate and aspartate might be responsible for the lower sensitivity of Shaker-iVSD to Zn2+, as we find ~40% of the current still at 20 µM, at which Hv1 is already fully blocked (Takeshita et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference from experimental observation and comparison with literature

claim: Wild type Shaker channels are stabilized in the closed state by external (300 µM) Zn2+.
source: Wild type Shaker channels are stabilized in the closed state by external (300 µM) Zn2+ (Boland et al., 1994).

claim: The addition of external Zn2+ to Shaker-iVSD reduced and not increased the current at −90 mV.
source: However, the addition of external Zn2+ to Shaker-iVSD did reduce and not increase the current at −90 mV, suggesting that either binding of Zn2+ caused the voltage sensing domain to adopt its 'native' conformation (i.e. the non-conducting one in the full Shaker channel) or that the Zn2+ directly blocks the ion permeation pathway.

claim: The position of D277/E283 and E335 support the notion that the ion permeation follows the pathway through the gating pore like in Hv1 and ω-currents.
source: The position of D277/E283 and E335 – corresponding to H140 and H194 – support the notion that the ion permeation follows the pathway through the gating pore like in Hv1 and ω-currents.

claim: The voltage dependence of opening of Shaker-iVSD-D277H was shifted to more hyperpolarized potentials (V½ = −99 mV).
source: The voltage dependence of opening of Shaker-iVSD-D277H was shifted to more hyperpolarized potentials (V½ = −99 mV).

claim: Shaker-iVSD-D277H showed a 40-times higher affinity to Zn2+ with an IC50 of 0.15 µM versus 6 µM for Shaker-iVSD.
source: When blocking the currents with Zn2+, we found that the channel showed a 40-times higher affinity to Zn2+ with an IC50 of 0.15 µM versus 6 µM for Shaker-iVSD (Figure 3i), confirming the pathway through the gating pore in the central voltage sensor domain.

claim: The higher Zn2+ affinity of Shaker-iVSD-D277H confirms the pathway through the gating pore in the central voltage sensor domain.
source: When blocking the currents with Zn2+, we found that the channel showed a 40-times higher affinity to Zn2+ with an IC50 of 0.15 µM versus 6 µM for Shaker-iVSD (Figure 3i), confirming the pathway through the gating pore in the central voltage sensor domain.

claim: The fluorescence kinetics of Shaker-iVSD were slower than Shaker-W434F.
source: The resulting fluorescence kinetics of Shaker-iVSD were slower than Shaker-W434F (Figure 4a).

claim: At a holding potential of −90 mV, the channels were already in the open state, and they closed (or deactivated) very slowly upon depolarization.
source: At a holding potential of −90 mV, the channels were already in the open state, and they closed (or deactivated) very slowly upon depolarization.

claim: The corresponding fluorescence changes did not seem to correlate to the ionic current when holding at −90 mV.
source: The corresponding fluorescence changes did not seem to correlate to the ionic current.

claim: At a holding resting potential of 0 mV, the fluorescence developed slower than at −90 mV.
source: At a holding resting potential of 0 mV, it became more feasible to compare the slower development of the ionic currents (Figure 1c top) to the corresponding fluorescence changes (Figure 4a, center). The fluorescence developed slower than at −90 mV, and superposition of ionic current and fluorescence changes from simultaneous measurements showed that both current and fluorescence developed with similar time constants when pulsing to strongly hyperpolarized potentials (Figure 4b).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 4a and 4b

claim: Both current and fluorescence developed with similar time constants when pulsing to strongly hyperpolarized potentials from a holding potential of 0 mV.
source: At a holding resting potential of 0 mV, it became more feasible to compare the slower development of the ionic currents (Figure 1c top) to the corresponding fluorescence changes (Figure 4a, center). The fluorescence developed slower than at −90 mV, and superposition of ionic current and fluorescence changes from simultaneous measurements showed that both current and fluorescence developed with similar time constants when pulsing to strongly hyperpolarized potentials (Figure 4b).

claim: Fluorescence change and conduction are two independent steps.
source: The fact that the signals coincided during hyperpolarization (holding at 0 mV) but not during depolarization (holding at −90 mV) shows that fluorescence change and conduction are two independent steps.

claim: The step developing conduction is rate limiting only when holding at 0 mV.
source: The step developing conduction is rate limiting only when holding at 0 mV.

claim: From a holding potential of −90 mV, the iVSD first undergoes the fast conformational change, reported by the fluorescence that corresponds to the gating currents, before the channels close slowly.
source: From a holding potential of −90 mV, the iVSD first undergoes the fast conformational change, reported by the fluorescence that corresponds to the gating currents (Haddad and Blunck, 2011), before the channels close slowly.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations and citation

claim: When holding at 0 mV, iVSD first opens the channel (slow, conduction) before undergoing the normal gating movement (fast, fluorescence).
source: Conversely, when holding at 0 mV, iVSD first opens the channel (slow, conduction) before undergoing the normal gating movement (fast, fluorescence).

claim: The fluorescence follows the rate-limiting slow channel opening when holding at 0 mV.
source: The fluorescence now follows the rate-limiting slow channel opening.

claim: Activation kinetics of ionic current traces and fluorescence signals followed a bi-exponential function with a fast and a slow time constant.
source: In a more in-depth analysis activation kinetics of ionic current traces (as shown on the top left of Figure 1c) and fluorescence signals (as shown on the top of Figure 4) followed a bi-exponential function with a fast and a slow time constant (τfast and τslow, respectively, Figure 4c).

claim: The time constants were voltage-dependent and showed a typical bell shape with maxima at about −100 mV for fluorescence signals and −90 ~ −70 mV for ionic currents.
source: The time constants were voltage-dependent and showed a typical bell shape with maxima at about −100 mV for fluorescence signals and −90 ~ −70 mV for ionic currents.

claim: The time constants of current and fluorescence signal correlated well in the range where most of the ionic current developed (<−120 mV).
source: The time constants of current and fluorescence signal correlated well in the range where most of the ionic current developed (<−120 mV) whereas the ionic current developed slower at more depolarized potentials.

claim: The ionic current developed slower at more depolarized potentials.
source: The time constants of current and fluorescence signal correlated well in the range where most of the ionic current developed (<−120 mV) whereas the ionic current developed slower at more depolarized potentials.

claim: The processes associated to both time constants did not contribute equally to the fluorescence amplitudes.
source: Although we found the same time constants in current and fluorescence, the time courses did not superimpose directly (Figure 4b), indicating that the processes associated to both time constants did not contribute equally to the fluorescence amplitudes.

claim: The midpoint of activation was not significantly shifted in Shaker-iVSD compared to wild type.
source: In the fluorescence voltage-relation, the midpoint of activation was not significantly shifted in Shaker-iVSD compared to wild type, but the voltage dependence was much shallower, so much so that even at the extreme potentials the FV relation were not yet fully saturated (Figure 4d).

claim: The voltage dependence was much shallower in Shaker-iVSD, so much so that even at the extreme potentials the FV relation were not yet fully saturated.
source: In the fluorescence voltage-relation, the midpoint of activation was not significantly shifted in Shaker-iVSD compared to wild type, but the voltage dependence was much shallower, so much so that even at the extreme potentials the FV relation were not yet fully saturated (Figure 4d).

claim: The fluorescence voltage relations shifted by ~50 mV when holding at −90 mV versus 0 mV.
source: However, we have shown above that the kinetics of the fluorescence changes differed significantly when holding at −90 mV as compared to holding at 0 mV (Figure 4a). The differences also stretched towards the corresponding voltage dependences of the fluorescence voltage relations, which shifted by ~50 mV when holding at both voltages (Figure 5a).

claim: Such a hysteresis was earlier identified as 'relaxation' or 'mode shift'.
source: Such a hysteresis was earlier identified as 'relaxation' or 'mode shift' (Bruening-Wright and Larsson, 2007; Villalba-Galea et al., 2008).

claim: The pore domain contributes to the development of the mode shift.
source: We previously described that the pore domain contributes to the development of the mode shift (Haddad and Blunck, 2011) and it had been related to C-type inactivation (Olcese et al., 1997).

claim: Shaker-iVSD follows the hysteresis pattern, resolving the issue of whether relaxation is an intrinsic property of VSDs.
source: However, mode shift, or 'relaxation', was also observed in the voltage-gated phosphatase of C. intestinalis (Ci-VSP), which is devoid of a pore domain (Labro et al., 2012; Villalba-Galea et al., 2008), suggesting that it is an intrinsic property of voltage sensing domains. Our finding here resolves the issue since also Shaker-iVSD follows the hysteresis pattern.
evidence: Inference from experimental observation and comparison with literature

claim: The shift of the FV relations was more pronounced in Shaker-iVSD, shifting by −95 mV compared to −31 mV shift of Shaker-W434F.
source: Just like wild type Shaker channels, the FV relations were shifted to more hyperpolarized potentials when holding at depolarized potentials. The shift of the FV relations was more pronounced in Shaker-iVSD, shifting by −95 mV compared to −31 mV shift of Shaker-W434F (Figure 5b).

claim: The FV relations of Shaker-iVSD were continuously shifted to more hyperpolarized potentials at more depolarized holding potentials and did not saturate within the tested holding potentials.
source: The FV relations of Shaker-iVSD were continuously shifted to more hyperpolarized potentials at more depolarized holding potentials and did not saturate within the tested holding potentials.

claim: In Shaker-W434F, the shift already saturated at a holding potential of −30 mV.
source: In Shaker-W434F, the shift already saturated at a holding potential of −30 mV.

claim: For Shaker-iVSD, the resulting curve was mono-exponential with a time constant of 452 ms for entering mode shift.
source: For Shaker-iVSD, the resulting curve was mono-exponential with a time constant of 452 ms, whereas recovery from relaxation occurred in double-exponential fashion with time constants of 36 ms and 279 ms for Shaker-W434F (Figure 5c–e).

claim: Recovery from relaxation occurred in double-exponential fashion with time constants of 36 ms and 279 ms for Shaker-W434F.
source: For Shaker-iVSD, the resulting curve was mono-exponential with a time constant of 452 ms, whereas recovery from relaxation occurred in double-exponential fashion with time constants of 36 ms and 279 ms for Shaker-W434F (Figure 5c–e).

claim: The mode shift coincided temporally with the onset of the ionic current in Shaker-iVSD.
source: The mode shift coincided temporally with the onset of the ionic current in Shaker-iVSD (Figure 5f), indicating that the permeation pathway, although open in both resting and activated state, closes during relaxation of the voltage sensing domain.

claim: The permeation pathway, although open in both resting and activated state, closes during relaxation of the voltage sensing domain.

source: The conformational changes of the voltage sensing domain in the absence of the pore domain might be minor, but the development of a cation pore and the much slower kinetics in spite of the same primary sequence indicates that the stabilizing effects of the pore domain are essential for the native function.

claim: The final assembly does not necessarily behave like the sum of its components and might adopt a different conformation.
